explanation: VOR stations transmit in the VHF band from 108.00 to 117.95 MHz, just below the 118 MHz aviation voice band. Between 108 and 112 MHz they share the band with ILS localizers; kHz values would be far too low for VHF, and 329 to 335 MHz is glideslope.

stem: Lines drawn from the VOR station in a particular magnetic direction are:
explanation: A radial is a line of magnetic bearing extending outward from the VOR station, such as the 090 radial pointing due east magnetic. Bearings and headings describe the aircraft's direction or the direction to something, not lines originating at the station.

stem: The amplitude modulated variable phase signal and the frequency modulated reference phase signal of a Very-high-frequency Omnidirectional Range (VOR) station used for aircraft navigation are synchronized so that both signals are in phase with each other at ____________ of the VOR station.
explanation: The station is adjusted so the 30 Hz variable (AM) and reference (FM) signals are exactly in phase on the 360° magnetic north radial. Moving clockwise, the phase difference increases one degree per degree of magnetic bearing, which is how the receiver identifies the radial.

stem: What is the main underlying operating principle of the Very-high-frequency Omnidirectional Range (VOR) aircraft navigational system?
choices: A definite amount of time is required to send and receive a radio signal.
The difference between the peak values of two DC voltages may be used to determine an aircraft’s altitude above a selected VOR station.
A phase difference between two AC voltages may be used to determine an aircraft’s azimuth position in relation to a selected VOR station.
A phase difference between two AC voltages may be used to determine an aircraft’s distance from a selected VOR station.
explanation: A VOR receiver compares the phase of the 30 Hz variable signal with the 30 Hz reference signal, and the phase difference equals the aircraft's magnetic bearing from the station. VOR gives azimuth only; distance comes from DME, which is the system based on signal travel time.

stem: What is the frequency range of the localizer beam system used by aircraft to find the centerline of a runway during an Instrument Landing System (ILS) approach to an airport?
explanation: ILS localizers operate on 40 channels from 108.10 to 111.95 MHz, sharing that VHF segment with VORs. The 329.15 to 335.00 MHz band carries the paired glideslope, and the kHz ranges are far too low for VHF navigation.

stem: What is the frequency range of the marker beacon system used to indicate an aircraft's position during an Instrument Landing System (ILS) approach to an airport's runway?
choices: The outer, middle, and inner marker beacons’ UHF frequencies are unique for each ILS equipped airport to provide unambiguous frequency-protected reception areas in the 329.15 to 335.00 MHz range.
The outer marker beacon’s carrier frequency is 400 MHz, the middle marker beacon’s carrier frequency is 1300 MHz, and the inner marker beacon’s carrier frequency is 3000 MHz.
The outer, the middle, and the inner marker beacon’s carrier frequencies are all 75 MHz but the marker beacons are 95% tone-modulated at 400 Hz (outer), 1300 Hz (middle), and 3000 Hz (inner).
The outer, marker beacon’s carrier frequency is 3000 kHz, the middle marker beacon’s carrier frequency is 1300 kHz, and the inner marker beacon’s carrier frequency is 400 kHz.
explanation: All marker beacons transmit on 75 MHz, beamed straight up, so the receiver identifies them by their 400 Hz, 1300 Hz, and 3000 Hz tones for the outer, middle, and inner markers. The tones also light the blue, amber, and white marker lamps.

stem: Which of the following is a required component of an Instrument Landing System (ILS)?
choices: Altimeter: shows aircraft height above sea-level.
Localizer: shows aircraft deviation horizontally from center of runway.
VHF Communications: provide communications to aircraft.
Distance Measuring Equipment: shows aircraft distance to VORTAC station.
explanation: The localizer is a core ILS component, providing lateral guidance that shows deviation left or right of the runway centerline, while the glideslope supplies vertical guidance. Altimeters, VHF communication radios, and VORTAC distance equipment are separate aircraft systems, not required parts of the ILS.

stem: What type of antenna is used in an aircraft’s Instrument Landing System (ILS) glideslope installation?
choices: A vertically polarized antenna that radiates an omnidirectional antenna pattern.
An electronically steerable phased-array antenna that radiates a directional antenna pattern.
explanation: Glideslope signals in the 329.15 to 335 MHz UHF band are horizontally polarized and are received by a folded dipole, often mounted in the nose or radome. The aircraft antenna only receives, and the balanced loop is associated with the marker beacon receiver.

stem: Choose the only correct statement about the localizer beam system used by aircraft to find the centerline of a runway during an Instrument Landing System (ILS) approach to an airport. The localizer beam system:
choices: Operates within the assigned frequency range of 108.10 to 111.95 GHz.
Produces two amplitude modulated antenna patterns; one pattern above and one pattern below the normal 2.5 degree approach glide path of the aircraft.
Frequencies are automatically tuned-in when the proper glide slope frequency is selected on the aircraft’s Navigation and Communication (NAV/COMM) transceiver.

Produces two amplitude modulated antenna patterns; one pattern with an audio frequency of 90 Hz and one pattern with an audio frequency of 150 Hz, one left of the runway centerline and one right of the runway centerline.
explanation: The localizer radiates two overlapping AM patterns, one modulated at 90 Hz and one at 150 Hz, on opposite sides of the runway centerline. The receiver compares the two tone depths, and equal depth means the aircraft is on centerline. Patterns above and below the glide path describe the glideslope instead.

stem: On runway approach, an ILS Localizer shows:
choices: Deviation left or right of runway center line.
Deviation up and down from ground speed.
Deviation percentage from authorized ground speed.
explanation: The localizer provides lateral guidance only, driving the course deviation needle to show whether the aircraft is left or right of the runway centerline. Vertical guidance comes from the glideslope, and no ILS element measures ground speed or wind.

stem: What is the frequency range of an aircraft’s Automatic Direction Finding (ADF) equipment?
explanation: ADF receivers cover the LF/MF range from 190 to 1750 kHz, which takes in nondirectional beacons and AM broadcast stations. The 108 MHz ranges listed belong to VHF aids such as VOR and the localizer.

stem: What is meant by the term “night effect” when using an aircraft’s Automatic Direction Finding (ADF) equipment? Night effect refers to the fact that:
choices: All Non Directional Beacon (NDB) transmitters are turned-off at dusk and turned-on at dawn.
Non Directional Beacon (NDB) transmissions can bounce-off the Earth’s ionosphere at night and be received at almost any direction.
An aircraft’s ADF transmissions will be slowed at night due to the increased density of the Earth’s atmosphere after sunset.
An aircraft’s ADF antennas usually collect dew moisture after sunset which decreases their effective reception distance from an NDB transmitter.
explanation: At night the lowest, most absorbing ionospheric layer disappears, so LF/MF beacon signals reflect from higher ionospheric layers as skywaves and arrive from varying directions, mixing with the groundwave. The ADF needle then wanders or points erratically, especially around sunset and sunrise.

stem: What are the transmit and receive frequencies of an aircraft’s mode C transponder operating in the Air Traffic Control RADAR Beacon System (ATCRBS)?
choices: Transmit at 1090 MHz, and receive at 1030 MHz
Transmit at 1030 kHz, and receive at 1090 kHz
Transmit at 1090 kHz, and receive at 1030 kHz
Transmit at 1030 MHz, and receive at 1090 MHz
explanation: Ground ATCRBS interrogators transmit on 1030 MHz and aircraft transponders reply on 1090 MHz. So the airborne transponder receives at 1030 MHz and transmits at 1090 MHz; these are L-band frequencies, not kHz.

stem: In addition to duplicating the functions of a mode C transponder, an aircraft’s mode S transponder can also provide:
explanation: Mode S adds unique aircraft addressing and a digital data link. TCAS uses Mode S to interrogate nearby aircraft and to coordinate resolution advisories between aircraft, providing mid-air collision avoidance. A transponder does no primary radar, lightning detection, or voice relay.

stem: What type of encoding is used in an aircraft’s mode C transponder transmission to a ground station of the Air Traffic Control RADAR Beacon System (ATCRBS)?
explanation: A Mode C transponder's reply is a train of pulses between two framing pulses, with each code bit sent as the presence or absence of a pulse at a fixed time position. This pulse position modulation carries the pressure altitude or squawk code on 1090 MHz.

stem: Choose the only correct statement about an aircraft’s Automatic Direction Finding (ADF) equipment.
choices: An aircraft’s ADF transmission exhibits primarily a line-of-sight range to the ground-based target station and will not follow the curvature of the Earth.
Only a single omnidirectional sense antenna is required to receive an NDB transmission and process the signal to calculate the aircraft’s bearing to the selected ground station.
All frequencies in the ADF’s operating range except the commercial standard broadcast stations (550 to 1660 kHz) can be utilized as a navigational Non Directional Beacon (NDB) signal.
An aircraft’s ADF antennas can receive transmissions that are over the Earth’s horizon (sometimes several hundred miles away) since these signals will follow the curvature of the Earth.
explanation: ADF and NDB frequencies are LF/MF, where the groundwave follows the Earth's curvature, so beacons can be received beyond the horizon, sometimes hundreds of miles away. Line-of-sight limits apply at VHF and above, and the ADF only receives, using both loop and sense antennas.

stem: What type of antenna pattern is radiated from a ground station phased-array directional antenna when transmitting the PPM pulses in a Mode S interrogation signal of an aircraft’s Traffic alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) installation?
explanation: Interrogations, whether from a ground Mode S sensor or from TCAS, go out on 1030 MHz, and transponder replies come back on 1090 MHz. A phased-array antenna forms a steerable beam, so the interrogation pattern is directional rather than omnidirectional.

stem: What type of antenna is used in an aircraft’s Instrument Landing System (ILS) marker beacon installation?
choices: An electronically steerable phased-array antenna that radiates a directional antenna pattern.
A horizontally polarized antenna that radiates an omnidirectional antenna pattern.
explanation: Marker beacons beam their 75 MHz signal straight up in a narrow fan, so the aircraft needs only a belly-mounted receive antenna such as a balanced loop. The aircraft never radiates on the marker frequency, and the folded dipole is the glideslope receiving antenna.

stem: What is the frequency range of an aircraft’s Very High Frequency (VHF) communications?
choices: 118.000 MHz to 136.975 MHz (worldwide up to 151.975 MHz).
explanation: Civil aviation VHF voice uses AM from 118.000 to 136.975 MHz, and many transceivers offer extended tuning to 151.975 MHz for use in some regions. The 108 to 117.95 MHz band just below is reserved for VOR and localizer navigation.

stem: Aircraft Emergency Locator Transmitters (ELT) operate on what frequencies?
explanation: ELTs send a swept-tone homing signal on 121.5 MHz (civil emergency) and 243 MHz (military emergency), and modern units add a digital 406 MHz burst detected by COSPAS-SARSAT satellites. Satellites stopped processing 121.5 and 243 MHz in 2009, but those signals remain useful for homing.

stem: What is the frequency range of an aircraft’s radio altimeter?
explanation: Radio altimeters operate in the 4.2 to 4.4 GHz aeronautical band, typically sweeping 4250 to 4350 MHz, and compare the transmitted signal with the echo from the ground directly below to find height above terrain. The 962 to 1213 MHz range belongs to DME.

stem: What type of antenna is attached to an aircraft’s Mode C transponder installation and used to receive 1030 MHz interrogation signals from the Air Traffic Control Radar Beacon System (ATCRBS)?
choices: An electronically steerable phased-array directional antenna.
An L-band monopole blade-type omnidirectional antenna.
An internally mounted, mechanically rotatable loop antenna.
explanation: Transponders receive 1030 MHz interrogations and reply on 1090 MHz through a short, vertically polarized quarter-wave blade monopole, usually on the belly. Its omnidirectional pattern works regardless of where the ground station lies, and both frequencies sit in the L-band.

stem: Some aircraft and avionics equipment operates with a prime power line frequency of 400 Hz. What is the principle advantage of a higher line frequency?
choices: 400 Hz power supplies draw less current than 60 Hz supplies allowing more current available for other systems on the aircraft.
A 400 Hz power supply generates less heat and operates much more efficiently than a 60 Hz power supply.
The magnetic devices in a 400 Hz power supply such as transformers, chokes and filters are smaller and lighter than those used in 60 Hz power supplies.
400 Hz power supplies are much less expensive to produce than power supplies with lower line frequencies.
explanation: Transformer voltage is proportional to frequency × turns × core area × flux density, so at a higher frequency the same voltage needs less core. At 400 Hz, transformers, chokes, and filter components can be much smaller and lighter than at 60 Hz, a big advantage where weight matters.

stem: Aviation services use predominantly ____ microphones.
explanation: Aviation favors dynamic microphones because they are rugged, tolerate vibration, humidity, and temperature extremes, and need no polarizing voltage. Older carbon microphones are noisy and degrade with age, and crystal elements are fragile and sensitive to moisture.

stem: Typical airborne HF transmitters usually provide a nominal RF power output to the antenna of ____ watts, compared with ____ watts RF output from a typical VHF transmitter.
explanation: Long-range HF skywave contacts need more power, so airborne HF transmitters typically deliver about 100 W, while VHF transmitters reach far enough line-of-sight from altitude with about 20 W.

stem: Before ground testing an aircraft RADAR, the operator should:
choices: Ensure that the area in front of the antenna is clear of other maintenance personnel to avoid radiation hazards.
Be sure the receiver has been properly shielded and grounded.
First test the transmitter connected to a matched load.
Measure power supply voltages to prevent circuit damage.
explanation: Aircraft radar radiates high-power microwave energy that can injure people close to the antenna, so before ground testing the operator must confirm nobody is in the beam path. Protecting personnel comes before equipment checks such as power supply or dummy-load tests.

stem: What type of antenna is used in an aircraft’s Very High Frequency Omnidirectional Range (VOR) and Localizer (LOC) installations?
choices: Vertically polarized antenna that radiates an omnidirectional antenna pattern.
explanation: VOR and localizer signals are horizontally polarized, so the aircraft uses a horizontally polarized, omnidirectional receive antenna, typically a V-shaped dipole on the tail or fuselage. Vertically polarized antennas serve VHF communications, and the aircraft doesn't transmit on VOR frequencies.

stem: What is the function of a commercial aircraft’s SELCAL installation? SELCAL is a type of aircraft communications __________.
choices: Device that allows an aircraft’s receiver to be continuously calibrated for signal selectivity.
System where a ground-based transmitter can call a selected aircraft or group of aircraft without the flight crew monitoring the ground-station frequency.
Transmission that uses sequential logic algorithm encryption to prevent public “eavesdropping” of crucial aircraft flight data.
System where an airborne transmitter can selectively calculate the line-of-sight distance to several ground-station receivers.
explanation: SELCAL assigns each aircraft a unique four-tone code. When a ground station transmits that code, the aircraft's decoder triggers a chime or light, so crews on long HF routes can leave the noisy frequency muted until they are actually called.

stem: What is a 1/2 digit on a DMM?
choices: Smaller physical readout on the left side of the display.
Partial extended accuracy on lower part of the range.
Smaller physical readout on the right side.
explanation: A half digit is a leading digit that can show only 0 or 1, so a 3½-digit meter counts to 1999 instead of 999. Readings beginning with 1 get one extra digit of resolution, a partial extension that applies only to the lower portion of the next decade.

stem: A 50 microampere meter movement has an internal resistance of 2,000 ohms. What applied voltage is required to indicate half-scale deflection?
explanation: Half-scale deflection needs half the full-scale current, 25 µA. V = I × R = 25 µA × 2,000 Ω = 0.05 V; full-scale deflection would take 0.1 V.

stem: What is the purpose of a series multiplier resistor used with a voltmeter?
choices: It is used to increase the voltage-indicating range of the voltmeter.
A multiplier resistor is not used with a voltmeter.
It is used to decrease the voltage-indicating range of the voltmeter.
It is used to increase the current-indicating range of an ammeter, not a voltmeter.
explanation: A multiplier resistor in series with the meter movement drops most of the applied voltage, keeping the movement's current within its full-scale rating at a higher voltage. Its value is the desired full-scale voltage divided by the movement's full-scale current, minus the movement's resistance.

stem: What is the purpose of a shunt resistor used with an ammeter?
choices: A shunt resistor is not used with an ammeter.
It is used to decrease the ampere indicating range of the ammeter.
It is used to increase the ampere indicating range of the ammeter.
It is used to increase the voltage indicating range of the voltmeter, not the ammeter.
explanation: A low-value shunt in parallel with the meter movement carries most of the circuit current, so only a small, fixed fraction passes through the movement. That lets the ammeter read currents far larger than the movement's own full-scale rating.

stem: What instrument is used to indicate high and low digital voltage states?
explanation: A logic probe touched to a digital circuit node lights indicators for logic high, logic low, and often pulsing activity. Ohmmeters and meggers measure resistance and insulation, and a signal strength meter reads RF field, so none show logic states.

stem: What instrument may be used to verify proper radio antenna functioning?
explanation: An SWR meter in the feed line compares forward and reflected power; a low SWR shows the antenna and line present a good match to the transmitter. A high or changing reading points to a damaged antenna, connector, or cable.

stem: How is a frequency counter used?
choices: To provide reference points on an analog receiver dial thereby aiding in the alignment of the receiver.
To heterodyne the frequency being measured with a known variable frequency oscillator until zero beat is achieved, thereby indicating the unknown frequency.
To measure the deviation in an FM transmitter in order to determine the percentage of modulation.
To measure the time between events, or the frequency, which is the reciprocal of the time.
explanation: A frequency counter counts cycles or events against an accurate internal time base, measuring either events per second (frequency) or the time between events (period). Since frequency is the reciprocal of period, either measurement yields the other. Zero-beating against a variable oscillator describes a heterodyne frequency meter instead.

stem: What is a frequency standard?
choices: A well-known (standard) frequency used for transmitting certain messages.
A device used to produce a highly accurate reference frequency.
A device for accurately measuring frequency to within 1 Hz.
A device used to generate wide-band random frequencies.
explanation: A frequency standard is a very stable oscillator, such as an oven-controlled crystal, rubidium, or cesium source, that produces an accurate reference frequency. It is used to calibrate counters, signal generators, and transmitters rather than to measure unknown frequencies itself.

stem: What equipment may be useful to track down EMI aboard a ship or aircraft?
explanation: A portable AM receiver works as a sniffer: tuned between stations, it picks up the buzz or hash radiated by motors, switching supplies, and arcing contacts, getting louder as you approach the source. Meters, scopes, and logic probes need a direct connection and can't locate a radiating source this way.

stem: On an analog wattmeter, what part of the scale is most accurate and how much does that accuracy extend to the rest of the reading scale?
choices: The accuracy is only at full scale, and that absolute number reading is carried through to the rest of the range. The upper 1/3 of the meter is the only truly calibrated part.
The accuracy is constant throughout the entire range of the meter.
The accuracy is only there at the upper 5% of the meter, and is not carried through at any other reading.
The accuracy cannot be determined at any reading.
explanation: Analog meter accuracy is stated as a percentage of full scale, so the same absolute error applies at every reading: ±5% of a 100 W scale is ±5 W, which is 25% of a 20 W reading. Only the upper third of the scale keeps that error acceptably small.

stem: Which of the following frequency standards is used as a time base standard by field technicians?
explanation: Rubidium standards are compact, warm up quickly, and are far more stable than quartz, making them practical portable references for field work. Cesium beam standards are larger, costlier primary standards usually kept in labs, while quartz and LC oscillators drift more.

stem: Which of the following contains a multirange AF voltmeter calibrated in dB and a sharp, internal 1000 Hz bandstop filter, both used in conjunction with each other to perform quieting tests?
explanation: A SINAD meter measures receiver audio on a dB-calibrated AF voltmeter, then switches in a sharp 1000 Hz notch that removes the test tone, leaving only noise and distortion. The ratio of the two readings, (signal + noise + distortion) / (noise + distortion), gives SINAD for sensitivity and quieting tests.

stem: What is used to decrease circuit loading when using an oscilloscope?
explanation: A 10:1 probe places about 9 MΩ, with a compensating capacitor, in series with the scope's 1 MΩ input, so the circuit sees about 10 MΩ and far less capacitance. The signal is reduced by ten, but the circuit under test is disturbed much less.

stem: How does a spectrum analyzer differ from a conventional oscilloscope?
choices: The oscilloscope is used to display electrical signals while the spectrum analyzer is used to measure ionospheric reflection.
The oscilloscope is used to display electrical signals in the frequency domain while the spectrum analyzer is used to display electrical signals in the time domain.
The oscilloscope is used to display electrical signals in the time domain while the spectrum analyzer is used to display electrical signals in the frequency domain.
The oscilloscope is used for displaying audio frequencies and the spectrum analyzer is used for displaying radio frequencies.
explanation: An oscilloscope plots amplitude against time, showing waveform shape, while a spectrum analyzer plots amplitude against frequency, separating each carrier, harmonic, and spur. Both can handle audio or RF within their bandwidth, so the real difference is the time versus frequency domain.

stem: What stage determines the maximum frequency response of an oscilloscope?
explanation: The vertical amplifier must pass the input signal to the deflection system without loss, so its bandwidth sets the highest frequency the scope can display accurately. The time base only controls how fast the trace sweeps horizontally.

stem: What factors limit the accuracy, frequency response, and stability of an oscilloscope?
choices: Sweep oscillator quality and deflection amplifier bandwidth.
Tube face voltage increments and deflection amplifier voltage.
Sweep oscillator quality and tube face voltage increments.
Deflection amplifier output impedance and tube face frequency increments.
explanation: The sweep (time-base) oscillator's linearity and stability determine how accurately and steadily time is displayed, while the deflection amplifier's bandwidth sets frequency response and how faithfully fast waveforms are reproduced.

stem: An oscilloscope can be used to accomplish all of the following except:
choices: Measure electron flow with the aid of a resistor.
Measure phase difference between two signals.
Measure velocity of light with the aid of a light emitting diode.
explanation: A scope measures voltage directly, current from the voltage across a known resistor (I = V / R), and phase difference by comparing two traces or a Lissajous pattern. Measuring the speed of light with an LED is not a normal oscilloscope task, so it is the exception.

stem: What instrument is used to check the signal quality of a single-sideband radio transmission?
explanation: Viewing the SSB RF envelope on an oscilloscope, often during a two-tone test, reveals flat-topping, distortion, and carrier leakage. Field strength and signal level meters show only how strong the signal is, not the shape of its waveform.

stem: A(n) ____ and ____ can be combined to measure the characteristics of transmission lines. Such an arrangement is known as a time-domain reflectometer (TDR).
explanation: A TDR sends a fast pulse from a pulse generator down the line and displays the reflections on an oscilloscope. The delay to each reflection gives the distance to a fault, and its shape and polarity show whether it is an open, short, or impedance change.

stem: What does the horizontal axis of a spectrum analyzer display?
explanation: A spectrum analyzer sweeps across a frequency span, so the horizontal axis is frequency and each signal appears as a vertical line at its own frequency.

stem: What does the vertical axis of a spectrum analyzer display?
explanation: The vertical axis shows the amplitude, or power, of each frequency component, usually on a logarithmic dBm scale so strong carriers and weak spurs can be compared on the same display.

stem: What instrument is most accurate when checking antennas and transmission lines at the operating frequency of the antenna?
explanation: A frequency domain reflectometer sweeps across the antenna's actual operating band and measures reflections there, so it shows return loss and SWR where they matter, along with distance to faults. A TDR's broadband pulse can't reveal frequency-dependent behavior such as antenna resonance.

stem: What test instrument can be used to display spurious signals in the output of a radio transmitter?
explanation: A spectrum analyzer displays the transmitter output across a wide frequency span, so harmonics, parasitics, and other spurious emissions appear as separate signals whose levels can be measured. A wattmeter reads only total power.

stem: What instrument is commonly used by radio service technicians to monitor frequency, modulation, check receiver sensitivity, distortion, and to generate audio tones?
explanation: A service monitor, or communications test set, combines a signal generator, receiver, frequency and deviation meter, SINAD and distortion meter, and audio generator, often with a scope or spectrum display, in one unit designed for radio servicing.

stem: Can a P25 radio system be monitored with a scanner?
choices: Yes , regardless if it has P25 decoding or not.
Yes, if the scanner has P25 decoding.
Yes, but it must also have P26 decoding.
explanation: P25 sends voice as digitized vocoder data, so a scanner without P25 decoding hears only digital noise. A scanner with P25 decoding can reproduce the voice, though it still can't follow encrypted traffic.

stem: Which of the following answers is true?
choices: The RF Power reading on a CDMA (code division multiple access) radio will be very accurate on an analog power meter.
The RF Power reading on a CDMA radio is not accurate on an analog power meter.
Power cannot be measured using CDMA modulation.
explanation: CDMA signals are noise-like, with a high peak-to-average ratio and constantly changing power, so an analog or diode power meter calibrated for a steady carrier reads them inaccurately. A true average or RMS power sensor designed for digital modulation is needed.

stem: What is a common method used to program radios without using a “wired” connection?
choices: Using the ultraviolet from a programmed radio to repeat the programming in another.
Having the radio maker send down a programming signal via satellite.
explanation: Some radios have an infrared port, similar to a TV remote link, so programming data can be sent from a computer interface or another radio without a cable. Ultraviolet and satellite links are not used for radio programming.

stem: What is the common method for determining the exact sensitivity specification of a receiver?
choices: Measure the recovered audio for 12 dB of SINAD.
Measure the recovered audio for 10 dB of quieting.
Measure the recovered audio for 10 dB of SINAD.
Measure the recovered audio for 25 dB of quieting.
explanation: Standard receiver sensitivity is the RF input level, usually in µV, that produces 12 dB SINAD in the recovered audio, about 25% noise and distortion. It is the accepted TIA/EIA reference, while quieting tests are an older, less precise FM method.

stem: A communications technician would perform a modulation-acceptance bandwidth test in order to:
choices: Ascertain the audio frequency response of the receiver.
Determine whether the CTCSS in the receiver is operating correctly.
Verify the results from a 12 dB SINAD test.
Determine the effective bandwidth of a communications receiver.
explanation: The test sets the RF level 6 dB above the 12 dB SINAD sensitivity point, then raises the deviation of the test signal until SINAD falls back to 12 dB. The deviation reached shows how wide a signal the receiver can accept, its effective bandwidth.

stem: What is the maximum FM deviation for voice operation of a normal wideband channel on VHF and UHF?
explanation: Standard wideband 25 kHz FM voice channels on VHF and UHF allow ±5 kHz maximum deviation. Narrowband 12.5 kHz channels cut that to ±2.5 kHz.

stem: When soldering or working with CMOS electronics products or equipment, a wrist strap:
choices: Must have less than 100,000 ohms of resistance to prevent static electricity.
Cannot be used when repairing TTL devices.
Must be grounded to a water pipe.
Does not work well in conjunction with anti-static floor mats.
explanation: A grounded wrist strap keeps the technician's body at ground potential, continuously bleeding off static charge before it can punch through thin CMOS gate oxide. Its resistance must stay below 100,000 ohms so charge drains quickly; it connects to a proper ESD ground point, not a water pipe, and works fine with anti-static mats.

stem: Which of the following is the preferred method of cleaning solder from plated-through circuit-board holes?
choices: Use a soldering iron tip that has a temperature above 900 degrees F.
explanation: A vacuum desoldering tool, either a hand solder sucker or a powered station, pulls molten solder out of the plated-through hole without damaging the barrel or pads. Picks can tear the plating, excess heat lifts pads, and air jets spray solder onto the board.

stem: What is the proper way to cut plastic wire ties?
choices: With flush-cut diagonal pliers and cut flush.
explanation: Flush-cut diagonal pliers cut the tie level with its head, leaving no sharp stub to cut hands or nick nearby wire insulation. Knives and scissors risk damaging the cable, and semi-flush cutters leave a pointed edge.

stem: The ideal method of removing insulation from wire is:
explanation: A thermal stripper melts through the insulation with a heated element, so there is no blade to nick or scrape the conductor strands. Knives and mechanical strippers can score the wire, leaving a weak spot that may break under vibration.

stem: A “hot gas bonder” is used:
choices: To apply solder to the iron tip while it is heating the component.
To allow soldering both sides of the PC board simultaneously.
explanation: A hot gas bonder directs a stream of heated air or inert gas onto the joint, melting solder without any tool touching the component. That makes it suited to surface-mount and heat-sensitive parts.

stem: When repairing circuit board assemblies it is most important to:
choices: Use a dental pick to clear plated-through holes.
Bridge broken copper traces with solder.
explanation: Board repair sends clipped leads flying and can spatter molten solder, flux, and solvents, so protecting the eyes comes first. An eye injury can't be undone, while holding fixtures and tools are matters of technique.

stem: What color is the binder for pairs 51-75 in a 100-pair cable?
explanation: In a 100-pair cable each 25-pair group is wrapped in a binder following the standard color sequence: blue for pairs 1–25, orange for 26–50, green for 51–75, and brown for 76–100.

stem: What is most important when routing cables in a mobile unit?
choices: That cables be cut to the exact length.
Assuring accessibility of the radio for servicing from outside the vehicle.
Assuring radio or electronics cables do not interfere with the normal operation of the vehicle.
Assuring cables are concealed under floor mats or carpeting.
explanation: Cables must stay clear of pedals, steering, airbags, seat tracks, and other moving or hot parts so the radio installation never interferes with safe vehicle operation. Burying them under floor mats invites crushing and chafing.

stem: Why should you not use white or translucent plastic tie wraps on a radio tower?
choices: White tie wraps are not FAA approved.
UV radiation from the Sun deteriorates the plastic very quickly.
The black tie wraps may cause electrolysis.
explanation: Ordinary white or natural nylon ties lack UV inhibitors, so sunlight makes them brittle and they fail quickly on an exposed tower. Black ties contain carbon black, which blocks UV and lets them last for years outdoors.

stem: What is the 6th pair color code in a 25 pair switchboard cable as is found in building telecommunications interconnections?
explanation: Pairs combine five primary colors (white, red, black, yellow, violet) with five secondary colors (blue, orange, green, brown, slate). Pairs 1–5 use white; pair 6 starts the red group with blue, so its tip is red with blue marking and its ring is blue with red marking.

stem: What tolerance off of plumb should a single base station radio rack be installed?
choices: Just outside the bubble on a level.
All the way to one end.
Just inside the bubble on a level.
explanation: A rack installed with the level's bubble just inside the marks is plumb within practical limits, so it stands stable, loads its base evenly, and doors and equipment hang properly. A bubble outside the marks means the rack is out of plumb.

stem: What type of wire would connect an SSB automatic tuner to an insulated backstay?
explanation: The lead from an SSB automatic tuner to an insulated backstay carries very high RF voltage, so it needs heavily insulated single-conductor GTO-15 high-voltage cable that won't arc through. Coax such as RG-8 or RG-213 runs from the transceiver to the tuner, not to the radiating element.

stem: On a 150 watt marine SSB HF transceiver, what would be indicated by a steady output of 75 watts when keying the transmitter on?
choices: There is probably a defect in the system causing the carrier to be transmitted.
One of the sidebands is missing.
explanation: A J3E SSB transmitter suppresses the carrier, so it should produce essentially no output when keyed without speech. A steady 75 W with no audio means a carrier is being transmitted, pointing to a fault such as an unbalanced modulator.

stem: The tachometer of a building’s elevator circuit experiences interference caused by the radio system nearby. What is a common potential “fix” for the problem?
choices: Replace the tachometer of the elevator.
Add a .01 µF capacitor across the motor/tachometer leads.
Add a 200 µF capacity across the motor/tachometer leads.
Add an isolating resistor in series with the motor leads.
explanation: A 0.01 µF capacitor has very low reactance at radio frequencies but high reactance at the low frequencies of the tach signal, so it bypasses RF picked up on the leads without upsetting the circuit. A 200 µF capacitor would load the circuit heavily.

stem: A common method of programming portable or mobile radios is to use a:
explanation: Modern portable and mobile radios are programmed with the manufacturer's software running on a laptop or PC, connected through a programming cable or interface, to load channels, tones, and features. Dummy loads, wattmeters, and signal generators are test equipment, not programming tools.

stem: In a software-defined transceiver, what would be the best way for a technician to make a quick overall evaluation of the radio’s operational condition?
choices: Set up a spectrum analyzer and service monitor and manually verify the manufacturer’s specifications.
Use another radio on the same frequency to check the transmitter.
Using on-board self-test routines are strictly prohibited by the FCC in commercial transmitters. Amateur Radio is the only service currently authorized to use them.
explanation: Software-defined radios usually include self-test routines that check the synthesizer, DSP, power stages, and other functions and report faults, giving a quick overall health check. A full bench verification takes far longer, and no FCC rule forbids self-tests in commercial radios.

stem: How might an installer verify correct GPS sentence to marine DSC VHF radio?
choices: Press and hold the red distress button.
Look for latitude and longitude on the display.
Ask for VHF radio check position report.
explanation: When valid GPS NMEA data reaches the DSC radio, it shows the vessel's current latitude and longitude, often with time, on the display. If no position appears, check the wiring and sentence format; never press the distress button to test.

stem: What steps must be taken to activate the DSC emergency signaling function on a marine VHF?
explanation: DSC calls identify the sender by its 9-digit MMSI, so the distress function stays disabled until a registered MMSI is entered. A GPS input is strongly recommended so alerts include position, but the MMSI is what enables DSC.

stem: What term describes a wide-bandwidth communications system in which the RF carrier frequency varies according to some predetermined sequence?
explanation: Spread spectrum spreads a signal across a band far wider than the information needs, for example by hopping the carrier frequency in a predetermined pseudo-random sequence. A receiver that knows the same sequence follows it and recovers the signal.

stem: Name two types of spread spectrum systems used in most RF communications applications?
explanation: Direct sequence spreads the signal by combining the data with a fast pseudo-random chip code, while frequency hopping moves the carrier among many channels in a pseudo-random pattern. AM, FM, QPSK, QAM, and APSK are modulation types, not spreading methods.

stem: What is the term used to describe a spread spectrum communications system where the center frequency of a conventional carrier is altered many times per second in accordance with a pseudo-random list of channels?
explanation: Frequency hopping jumps the carrier from channel to channel many times per second, following a pseudo-random list known to both ends. Direct sequence instead keeps the center frequency fixed and spreads the signal with a high-rate chip code.

stem: A TDMA radio uses what to carry the multiple conversations sequentially?
explanation: Time division multiple access divides one radio channel into repeating time slots, and each conversation transmits in short bursts in its own slot. Two-slot TDMA, for example, carries two talk paths on a single frequency.

stem: Which of the following statements about SSB voice transmissions is correct?
choices: They use A3E emission which are produced by modulating the final amplifier.
They use F3E emission which is produced by phase shifting the carrier.
They normally use J3E emissions, which consists of one sideband and a suppressed carrier.
They may use A1A emission to suppress the carrier.
explanation: SSB voice normally uses J3E: one sideband with the carrier suppressed, saving power and bandwidth compared with full AM. A3E is double-sideband AM with full carrier, F3E is FM, and A1A is on-off keyed Morse telegraphy.

stem: What are the two most-used PCS (Personal Communications Systems) coding techniques used to separate different calls?
explanation: Second-generation PCS networks used two competing schemes: CDMA, which separates calls by giving each a unique spreading code, and GSM, which separates them in TDMA time slots on 200 kHz carriers. QPSK and QAM are modulation formats, not ways of separating calls.

stem: What is a CODEC?
choices: A device to read Morse code.
A computer operated digital encoding compandor.
A coder/decoder IC or circuitry that converts a voice signal into a predetermined digital format for encrypted transmission.
explanation: A codec, short for coder/decoder, converts analog voice into a defined digital format for transmission, where it can be encrypted, and converts received digital data back into audio. It is not a Morse reader or simply a compression chip.

stem: The GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) uses what type of CODEC for digital mobile radio system communications?
explanation: GSM's original full-rate speech codec is RPE-LTP, regular-pulse excitation with long-term prediction, which compresses speech to 13 kbit/s for transmission over the TDMA radio link.

stem: Which of the following codes has gained the widest acceptance for exchange of data from one computer to another?
explanation: ASCII, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, is the 7-bit character code adopted almost universally for computer data exchange. Baudot is a 5-bit teleprinter code, Gray code is used in position encoders, and Morse is for manual telegraphy.

stem: The International Organization for Standardization has developed a seven-level reference model for a packet-radio communications structure. What level is responsible for the actual transmission of data and handshaking signals?
explanation: The physical layer, layer 1 of the OSI model, handles the actual transmission of raw bits over the medium, including the radio or modem hardware and handshaking signals. The transport layer manages end-to-end delivery, and the model has no communications or synchronization layer.

stem: What CODEC is used in Phase 2 P25 radios?
explanation: Phase 2 P25 uses the AMBE+2 half-rate vocoder, which fits digitized voice into one TDMA time slot so two talk paths share a 12.5 kHz channel. Phase 1 radios originally used the full-rate IMBE vocoder.

stem: The International Organization for Standardization has developed a seven-level reference model for a packet-radio communications structure. The _______ level arranges the bits into frames and controls data flow.
explanation: The data link layer, layer 2 of the OSI model, groups bits into frames, adds addressing and error checking, and manages flow control between adjacent stations. In amateur packet radio, the AX.25 protocol works at this layer.

stem: What is a SDR?
explanation: SDR stands for software-defined radio: filtering, modulation, and demodulation are done by software on a DSP or processor rather than in fixed hardware, so the radio can be reconfigured by changing its software.

stem: What does the DSP not do in a modern DSP radio?
explanation: A DSP radio's processor handles frequency control, modulation, and detection, but SWR depends on the impedance match between transmitter, feed line, and antenna. The DSP can measure SWR, yet only antenna work or a tuner can change it.

stem: Which statement best describes the code used for GMDSS-DSC transmissions?
choices: A 10 bit error correcting code starting with bits of data followed by a 3 bit error correcting code.
A 10 bit error correcting code starting with a 3 bit error correcting code followed by 7 bits of data.
An 8 bit code with 7 bits of data followed by a single parity bit.
A 7 bit code that is transmitted twice for error correction.
explanation: Each DSC character is a 10-bit word: 7 information bits followed by 3 check bits that give, as a binary number, how many of the information bits are zeros. Any mismatch flags an error, and each character is also sent twice for time diversity.

stem: Which is the code used for SITOR-A and -B transmissions?
choices: Each character consists of 7 bits with 3 “zeros” and 4 “ones”.
Each character consists of 7 bits with 4 “zeros” and 3 “ones”.
Each character has 7 bits of data and 3 bits for error correction.
explanation: SITOR uses a 7-unit constant-ratio code in which every valid character has exactly four 0s and three 1s. A received character that breaks this 4:3 ratio is detected as an error, prompting a repeat in ARQ mode or use of the second copy in FEC mode.

stem: Which of the following statements is true?
choices: The Signal Repetition character (1001100) is used as a control signal in SITOR-ARQ.
The Idle Signal (a) (0000111) is used for FEC Phasing Signal 1.
The Idle Signal (b) (0011001) is used for FEC Phasing Signal 2.
The Control Signal 1 (0101100) is used to determine the time displacement in SITOR-B.
explanation: In SITOR-B (FEC), a run of phasing signals precedes traffic so the receiver can lock onto character timing, and Idle Signal alpha (0000111) is used as Phasing Signal 1. Control Signal 1 is an ARQ acknowledgment, while SITOR-B time diversity comes from a fixed spacing between each character and its repeat.

stem: What principle allows multiple conversations to be able to share one radio channel on a GSM channel?
explanation: GSM divides each 200 kHz carrier into eight repeating time slots, so up to eight conversations take turns on one channel, each transmitting in its own slot. That is time division multiplexing, not frequency division or double sideband.

stem: What is the channel spacing used for VHF marine radio?
explanation: Marine VHF channels in the 156–162 MHz band are spaced 25 kHz apart, which leaves room for FM signals with ±5 kHz deviation without spilling into the next channel.

stem: What VHF channel is assigned for distress and calling?
explanation: Channel 16 (156.800 MHz) is the international VHF frequency for distress, urgency, safety and calling. Channel 70 is a common trap: it carries only digital selective calling, never voice.

stem: What VHF Channel is used for Digital Selective Calling and acknowledgement?
explanation: Channel 70 (156.525 MHz) is reserved exclusively for digital selective calling, including distress alerts, routine calls and acknowledgments. Voice is prohibited there; follow-up voice traffic moves to channel 16 or a working channel.

stem: Maximum allowable frequency deviation for VHF marine radios is:
explanation: Marine VHF uses FM with peak deviation limited to ±5 kHz. With 3 kHz audio, Carson's rule gives BW = 2(Δf + f<sub>m</sub>) = 2(5 + 3) = 16 kHz, which fits comfortably inside a 25 kHz channel.

stem: What is the reason for the USA-INT control or function?
choices: It changes channels that are normally simplex channels into duplex channels.
It changes some channels that are normally duplex channels into simplex channels.
When the control is set to “INT” the range is increased.
explanation: Some international duplex channels are used as simplex channels in U.S. waters. In USA mode the radio transmits and receives on the ship frequency for those channels; INT mode restores international duplex operation and has no effect on range.

stem: How might an installer verify correct GPS sentence to marine DSC VHF radio?
choices: Look for latitude and longitude, plus speed, on VHF display.
Press and hold the red distress button.
Ask for VHF radio check position report.
explanation: When the GPS's NMEA sentences reach the DSC radio correctly, the radio shows the vessel's latitude and longitude, often with speed and time, on its display. Pressing the distress button to test would send a false distress alert.

stem: What is a common occurrence when voice-testing an SSB aboard a boat?
choices: Ammeter fluctuates down with each spoken word.
Voltage panel indicator lamps may glow with each syllable.
Automatic tuner cycles on each syllable.
Minimal voltage drop seen at power source.
explanation: An SSB transmitter has no carrier and puts out power only as you speak, so RF output and DC current surge with every syllable. Those surges and stray RF on the boat's DC wiring can make voltage-panel indicator lamps glow in step with speech, while the ammeter swings up, not down.

stem: What might contribute to apparent low voltage on marine SSB transmitting?
explanation: If the black negative fuse blows, the SSB's return current must find another path, such as the coax shield, tuner and RF ground, whose resistance drops voltage under the heavy transmit load. Blowing the red positive fuse instead would simply shut the radio off.

stem: What type of wire connects an SSB automatic tuner to an insulated backstay?
explanation: The tuner's output to an insulated backstay carries very high RF voltage, so it uses GTO-15 high-voltage single-conductor cable, the heavily insulated type made for neon signs, to resist arcing. Coax such as RG-8U or RG-213 belongs between the transceiver and the tuner.

stem: Which of the following statements concerning SITOR communications is true?
choices: ARQ message transmissions are made in data groups consisting of three-character blocks.
ARQ transmissions are acknowledged by the Information Receiving Station only at the end of the message.
ARQ communications rely upon error correction by time diversity transmission and reception.
Forward error correction is an interactive mode.
explanation: SITOR ARQ sends text in blocks of three characters, each in a seven-unit constant-ratio code. The receiving station checks every block and immediately acknowledges it or requests a repeat, rather than waiting until the end of the message.

stem: The sequence ARQ, FEC, SFEC best corresponds to which of the following sequences?
choices: One-way communications to a single station, one-way communications to all stations, two-way communications.
One-way communications to all stations, two-way communications, one-way communications to a single station.
Two way communications, one-way communications to all stations, one-way communications to a single station.
Two way communications, one-way communications to a single station, one-way communications to all stations.
explanation: ARQ is two-way, with every block acknowledged by the receiving station. FEC (collective mode) is one-way to all stations, and selective FEC (SFEC) is one-way to a single addressed station.

stem: Which of the following statements concerning SITOR communications is true?
choices: Communication is established on the working channel and answerbacks are exchanged before FEC broadcasts can be received.
In the ARQ mode each character is transmitted twice.
Weather broadcasts cannot be made in FEC because sending each character twice would cause the broadcast to be prohibitively long.
Two-way communication with the coast radio station using FEC is not necessary to be able to receive the broadcasts.
explanation: FEC broadcasts are one-way: each character is sent twice with time diversity, and receivers decode without replying. No link setup or answerback exchange with the coast station is needed, which is why weather and safety broadcasts use FEC.

keyTopicTitle: Survival Craft Equipment: VHF, SARTs & EPIRBs
stem: What causes the SART to begin a transmission?
choices: When activated manually, it begins radiating immediately.
After being activated the SART responds to RADAR interrogation.
It is either manually or water activated before radiating.
It begins radiating only when keyed by the operator.
explanation: Once switched on, the SART sits in standby and stays silent until a 9 GHz X-band radar pulse interrogates it; only then does it transmit its response. Activation alone doesn't make it radiate.

keyTopicTitle: Survival Craft Equipment: VHF, SARTs & EPIRBs
stem: How should the signal from a Search And Rescue RADAR Transponder appear on a RADAR display?
choices: A series of spirals all originating from the range and bearing of the SART.
A series of 12 equally spaced dots.
explanation: When interrogated, the SART sweeps through the 9 GHz radar band 12 times, so the radar shows a line of 12 equally spaced dots extending outward along the SART's bearing. As the ship closes within about a mile, the dots become arcs and then circles.

keyTopicTitle: Survival Craft Equipment: VHF, SARTs & EPIRBs
stem: In which frequency band does a search and rescue transponder operate?
explanation: The SART answers ship and aircraft X-band radars, so it operates around 9.2 to 9.5 GHz, the 9 GHz band. 406 MHz belongs to satellite EPIRBs, and 3 GHz S-band radars will not trigger a radar SART.

keyTopicTitle: Survival Craft Equipment: VHF, SARTs & EPIRBs
stem: Which piece of required GMDSS equipment is the primary source of transmitting locating signals?
explanation: The 406 MHz EPIRB is the GMDSS locating beacon: COSPAS-SARSAT satellites detect its bursts, determine its position and relay the alert to rescue authorities. SARTs work at 9 GHz, not 406 MHz, and only help with final homing.

keyTopicTitle: Survival Craft Equipment: VHF, SARTs & EPIRBs
stem: Which of the following statements concerning satellite EPIRBs is true?
choices: Once activated, these EPIRBs transmit a signal for use in identifying the vessel and for determining the position of the beacon.
The coded signal identifies the nature of the distress situation.
The coded signal only identifies the vessel’s name and port of registry.
If the GMDSS Radio Operator does not program the EPIRB, it will transmit default information such as the follow-on communications frequency and mode.
explanation: Each 406 MHz burst carries a coded identity registered to the vessel, and the satellite system uses the signal to fix the beacon's position, by Doppler measurement or from GPS data the beacon includes. The code does not describe the nature of the distress.

keyTopicTitle: Survival Craft Equipment: VHF, SARTs & EPIRBs
stem: What statement is true regarding 406 MHz EPIRB transmissions?
choices: Allows immediate voice communications with the RCC.
Coding permits the SAR authorities to know if manually or automatically activated.
Transmits a unique hexadecimal identification number.
Radio Operator programs an I.D. into the SART immediately prior to activation.
explanation: Every 406 MHz beacon transmits a unique 15-character hexadecimal identification code, registered with NOAA in the U.S., that links the alert to the vessel and its emergency contacts. The transmission is a digital data burst, not a voice channel.

stem: What is facsimile?
choices: The transmission of still pictures by slow-scan television.
The transmission of characters by radioteletype that form a picture when printed.
The transmission of printed pictures for permanent display on paper.
The transmission of video by television.
explanation: Facsimile scans a printed image line by line, transmits it, and reproduces it on paper at the receiving end for permanent display; weather charts are the classic marine example.

stem: What is the standard scan rate for high-frequency 3 MHz - 23 MHz weather facsimile reception from shore stations?
explanation: HF radiofacsimile broadcasts from shore stations, such as NOAA weather charts, use the standard rate of 120 lines per minute with an index of cooperation of 576, so receivers must be set to match.

stem: What would be the bandwidth of a good crystal lattice band-pass filter for weather facsimile HF (high frequency) reception?
explanation: HF weather fax uses FSK with an 800 Hz shift (center ±400 Hz), so a filter about 1 kHz wide at −6 dB passes the whole signal while rejecting noise and adjacent stations. Much wider filters admit needless noise; narrower ones clip the tones.

stem: Which of the following statements about NAVTEX is true?
choices: Receives MSI broadcasts using SITOR-B or FEC mode.
The ship station transmits on 518 kHz.
The ship receives MSI broadcasts using SITOR-A or ARQ mode.
NAVTEX is received on 2182 kHz using SSB.
explanation: NAVTEX coast stations broadcast maritime safety information one-way in SITOR FEC (collective) mode, and ships only receive, mainly on 518 kHz. Ships never transmit NAVTEX, and ARQ isn't used because it requires two-way handshaking.

stem: Which of the following is the primary frequency that is used exclusively for NAVTEX broadcasts internationally?
explanation: 518 kHz is the international NAVTEX frequency, used worldwide for English-language navigational and meteorological warnings. 490 kHz and 4209.5 kHz carry national-language and HF NAVTEX, and 2187.5 kHz is a DSC distress frequency.

stem: What determines whether a NAVTEX receiver does not print a particular type of message content?
choices: The message does not concern your vessel.
The subject indicator matches that programmed for rejection by the operator.
The transmitting station ID covering your area has not been programmed for rejection by the operator.
All messages sent during each broadcast are printed.
explanation: Each NAVTEX message header contains a transmitter identity and a subject-indicator character. The operator can program the receiver to reject chosen subject types, though navigational warnings, meteorological warnings and search-and-rescue messages can't be rejected.

stem: What data language is bi-directional, multi-transmitter, multi-receiver network?
explanation: NMEA 2000 is a CAN-based network running at 250 kbps, where many devices talk and listen in both directions on one shared backbone. NMEA 0183, by contrast, is a one-talker, multiple-listener serial link.

stem: How should shielding be grounded on an NMEA 0183 data line?
choices: Terminated to ground at the talker and unterminated at the listener.
Unterminated at the talker and terminated at the listener.
Terminated at both the talker and listener.
explanation: Ground the NMEA 0183 cable shield at the talker end only and leave it unconnected at the listener. Grounding both ends can create a ground loop that injects noise into the data line.

stem: What might occur in NMEA 2000 network topology if one device in line should fail?
choices: The system shuts down until the device is removed.
Other electronics after the failed device will be inoperable.
The main fuse on the backbone may open.
There will be no interruption to all other devices.
explanation: Each NMEA 2000 device connects to the backbone through a tee and drop cable, so the backbone itself stays continuous. When one device fails, the remaining devices keep communicating without interruption.

stem: In an NMEA 2000 device, a load equivalence number (LEN) of 1 is equivalent to how much current consumption?
explanation: One LEN equals 50 mA of current draw, rounded up to the next whole number. For example, a device drawing 300 mA has LEN = 300 mA ÷ 50 mA = 6.

stem: An NMEA 2000 system with devices in a single location may be powered using this method:
choices: No 12 volts needed for NMEA 2000 devices.
explanation: When all devices are clustered in one place, feeding power at one end of the backbone keeps the cable run between supply and loads short and the voltage drop small. Mid-powering is for loads spread along a longer backbone.

stem: What voltage drop at the end of the last segment will satisfy NMEA 2000 network cabling plans?
explanation: NMEA 2000 design rules limit the voltage drop from the power connection to the farthest device to 1.5 volts, so every device still gets adequate voltage even when the battery runs low. Larger drops call for heavier cable or mid-powering.

stem: What is the normal range of pulse repetition rates?
explanation: Marine radars typically pulse 500 to 2,000 times per second: lower rates on long ranges so echoes return before the next pulse, higher rates on short ranges for more hits on each target per sweep.

stem: The RADAR range in nautical miles to an object can be found by measuring the elapsed time during a RADAR pulse and dividing this quantity by:
explanation: Radio waves cover one nautical mile out and back in 12.346 µs, so range in nautical miles = elapsed time ÷ 12.346 µs. For example, 123.46 µs ÷ 12.346 µs = 10 nautical miles.

stem: What is the normal range of pulse widths?
explanation: Marine radar pulse widths run from about 0.05 µs on the shortest ranges to about 1.0 µs on long ranges. Short pulses give fine range resolution; longer pulses put more energy on distant targets.

stem: Shipboard RADAR is most commonly operated in what band?
explanation: Most ship radars operate in the X-band near 9.4 GHz, within the SHF range of 3 to 30 GHz; S-band sets near 3 GHz sit at its lower edge.

stem: The pulse repetition rate (prr) of a RADAR refers to the:
choices: Pulse rate of the local oscillator.
explanation: The magnetron is the radar's transmitting oscillator and fires once for every trigger pulse, so the pulse repetition rate is simply how many magnetron pulses occur per second. Duty cycle equals pulse width × PRR, not its reciprocal.

stem: If the elapsed time for a RADAR echo is 62 microseconds, what is the distance in nautical miles to the object?
explanation: Each nautical mile of range takes 12.346 µs for the round trip, so range = elapsed time ÷ 12.346 µs = 62 ÷ 12.346 ≈ 5.02, about 5 nautical miles.

stem: The ATR box:
choices: Prevents the received signal from entering the transmitter.
Protects the receiver from strong RADAR signals.
Turns off the receiver when the transmitter is on.
explanation: The anti-transmit-receive (ATR) tube sits in the transmitter branch of the duplexer; during reception it stays unfired and blocks returning echoes from being absorbed by the magnetron, steering them to the receiver. Protecting the receiver from the transmitted pulse is the TR tube's job.

stem: What is the purpose or function of the RADAR duplexer/circulator? It is a/an:
choices: Coupling device that is used in the transition from a rectangular waveguide to a circular waveguide.
Electronic switch that allows the use of one antenna for both transmission and reception.
Modified length of waveguide that is used to sample a portion of the transmitted energy for testing purposes.
Dual section coupling device that allows the use of a magnetron as a transmitter.
explanation: The duplexer, often a ferrite circulator, routes the magnetron's high-power pulse to the antenna and directs returning echoes to the receiver. This switching action lets one antenna serve for both transmission and reception.

stem: What device can be used to determine the performance of a RADAR system at sea?
explanation: An echo box is a high-Q resonant cavity that absorbs part of the transmitted pulse and rings it back to the receiver. The length of the resulting plume on the display shows overall transmitter power and receiver sensitivity, even with no targets available.

stem: What is the purpose of a synchro transmitter and receiver?
choices: Synchronizes the transmitted and received pulse trains.
Prevents the receiver from operating during the period of the transmitted pulse.
Transmits the angular position of the antenna to the indicator unit.
Keeps the speed of the motor generator constant.
explanation: Geared to the rotating antenna, the synchro transmitter sends its shaft angle electrically to a synchro receiver in the indicator, keeping the display's sweep in step with the antenna's bearing.

stem: Digital signal processing (DSP) of RADAR signals (compared with analog) causes:
choices: Improved weak signal or target enhancement.
Less interference with other radio communications equipment.
explanation: Once echoes are digitized, the processor can correlate and average them over many sweeps, suppressing random noise and clutter while reinforcing targets that return consistently, so weak targets stand out more clearly.

stem: The component or circuit providing the transmitter output power for a RADAR system is the:
explanation: The magnetron is a crossed-field oscillator that generates the high-power microwave pulses the antenna radiates. Thyratrons and SCRs only switch the modulator pulse, and klystrons in older radars served as the low-power receiver local oscillator.

stem: When a RADAR is being operated on the 48 mile range setting, what is the most appropriate pulse width (PW) and pulse repetition rate (pps)?
explanation: Long ranges need a wide pulse for more energy on distant targets and a slow rate so echoes return before the next pulse. At 500 pps, R<sub>max</sub> = (1 ÷ 500) ÷ 12.346 µs = 2,000 µs ÷ 12.346 µs ≈ 162 nmi; 2,000 pps would allow only about 40 nmi.

stem: When a RADAR is being operated on the 6 mile range setting what is the most appropriate pulse width and pulse repetition rate?
explanation: Six miles is a short-to-medium range, so a moderately narrow 0.25 µs pulse gives good range resolution and a 1,000 pps rate gives plenty of hits per sweep. Its 1,000 µs interval still covers 1,000 ÷ 12.346 ≈ 81 nmi, far beyond 6 miles.

stem: We are looking at a target 25 miles away. When a RADAR is being operated on the 25 mile range setting what is the most appropriate pulse width and pulse repetition rate?
explanation: At 25 miles, detecting weak distant echoes matters more than fine resolution, so a wide 1.0 µs pulse delivers more energy, and a slow 500 pps rate leaves ample listening time between pulses.

stem: What pulse width and repetition rate should you use at long ranges?
choices: Narrow pulse width and slow repetition rate.
Narrow pulse width and fast repetition rate.
Wide pulse width and fast repetition rate.
Wide pulse width and slow repetition rate.
explanation: Wide pulses carry more energy to detect weak, distant echoes, and a slow repetition rate leaves time for those echoes to return before the next pulse, avoiding range ambiguity and keeping the magnetron's duty cycle within limits.

stem: What pulse width and repetition rate should you use at short ranges?
choices: Wide pulse width and fast repetition rate.
Narrow pulse width and slow repetition rate.
Narrow pulse width and fast repetition rates.
Wide pulse width and slow repetition rates.
explanation: Narrow pulses give fine range resolution and a short minimum range for nearby targets, and a fast repetition rate puts more pulses on each target per sweep for a brighter, steadier picture. Close echoes return quickly, so there's no range ambiguity.

stem: When a RADAR is being operated on the 1.5 mile range setting, what is the most appropriate pulse width and pulse repetition rate?
explanation: On the 1.5 mile range the shortest pulse gives the best minimum range and resolution: c·τ ÷ 2 = (3×10⁸ × 0.05×10⁻⁶) ÷ 2 = 7.5 m. Then a fast 2,000 pps rate paints many hits on each target per sweep.

stem: How does the gain of a parabolic dish antenna change when the operating frequency is doubled?
explanation: Dish gain is G = η(πd/λ)². Doubling the frequency halves λ, so gain rises by 2² = 4 times, and 10 log 4 ≈ 6 dB.

stem: What type of antenna or pickup device is used to extract the RADAR signal from the wave guide?
explanation: The J-hook is a hook-shaped coupling element that picks the microwave energy out of the waveguide. Circulators only route energy among their ports, and a folded dipole is a wire antenna for much lower frequencies.

stem: What happens to the beamwidth of an antenna as the gain is increased? The beamwidth:
choices: Increases geometrically as the gain is increased.
Increases arithmetically as the gain is increased.
Is essentially unaffected by the gain of the antenna.
Decreases as the gain is increased.
explanation: Gain comes from concentrating radiated power into a narrower beam, so beamwidth shrinks as gain rises. For a dish, beamwidth ≈ 70λ/d degrees while gain grows with (d/λ)², so the two move in opposite directions.

stem: A common shipboard RADAR antenna is the:
explanation: Most ship radars use a rotating slotted waveguide array: slots cut along a length of waveguide radiate in phase, forming a narrow horizontal beam for sharp bearing resolution and a broad vertical beam that tolerates the ship's roll.

stem: Conductance takes place in a waveguide:
choices: In the same manner as a transmission line.
Through electromagnetic and electrostatic fields in the walls of the waveguide.
explanation: With no center conductor, a waveguide doesn't carry energy the way a transmission line does. Energy travels as electromagnetic and electrostatic (magnetic and electric) fields bounded by the conducting walls, which carry the induced currents.

stem: To couple energy into and out of a waveguide use:
choices: A thin piece of wire as an antenna.
explanation: Placed at an electric-field maximum inside the guide, a thin wire probe acts as a small antenna that launches energy into the waveguide or picks it out. Loops and slots are the other common coupling methods.

stem: The permanent magnetic field that surrounds a traveling-wave tube (TWT) is intended to:
choices: Prevent the electron beam from spreading.
explanation: Electrons in the beam repel one another, so the permanent-magnet focusing field around a traveling-wave tube keeps the beam narrow as it travels down the helix, maintaining interaction with the RF wave and keeping electrons off the helix.

stem: Prior to testing any RADAR system, the operator should first:
choices: Assure the display unit is operating normally.
Inform the airport control tower or ship’s master.
Assure no personnel are in front of the antenna.
explanation: Radar antennas radiate high-power microwaves that can heat body tissue, especially the eyes, so before transmitting make sure nobody is near or in front of the antenna. Personnel safety comes before any equipment check.

stem: In the term “ARPA RADAR,” ARPA is the acronym for which of the following?
explanation: ARPA stands for Automatic RADAR Plotting Aid, a radar function that automatically tracks selected targets and computes their course, speed, closest point of approach and time to it, for collision avoidance.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a precaution that should be taken to ensure the magnetron is not weakened:
choices: Keep metal tools away from the magnet.
Do not subject it to excessive heat.
Do not subject it to shocks and blows.
explanation: Magnetron output depends on its permanent magnet, which heat, mechanical shock and nearby steel tools can weaken. Tuning the TR (transmit-receive) cell protects the receiver and has nothing to do with the magnet, so it isn't a magnetron precaution.

stem: Exposure to microwave energy from RADAR or other electronics devices is limited by U.S. Health Department regulations to _______ mW/centimeter.
explanation: The long-standing federal microwave figure is 5 mW/cm²: it is the FDA's leakage limit for microwave ovens in use and matches the FCC occupational exposure limit above 1.5 GHz.

stem: RADAR collision avoidance systems utilize inputs from each of the following except your ship’s:
explanation: Collision avoidance needs own-ship heading from the gyrocompass, speed from the speed log and position from the navigation receiver to compute target courses and closest approach. Wind speed from an anemometer plays no part in target plotting.

stem: What is the orbiting altitude of the Iridium satellite communications system?
explanation: Iridium satellites fly in low Earth orbit about 780 km (485 miles) up, far below the roughly 22,000 mile geostationary altitude used by Inmarsat.

stem: What frequency band is used by the Iridium system for telephone and messaging?
explanation: Iridium user links to phones and terminals operate in L-band at 1616–1626 MHz, using the same band for both directions with time-division duplexing. Ka-band frequencies serve only the feeder links and satellite crosslinks.

stem: What services are provided by the Iridium system?
choices: Analog voice and Data at 4.8 kbps.
Digital voice and Data at 9.6 kbps.
Digital voice and Data at 2.4 kbps.
Analog voice and Data at 9.6 kbps.
explanation: Iridium is an all-digital system: voice is digitally coded, and its basic circuit-switched data service runs at 2.4 kbps. No analog voice is carried.

stem: Which of the following statements about the Iridium system is true?
choices: There are 48 spot beams per satellite with a footprint of 30 miles in diameter.
There are 48 satellites in orbit in 4 orbital planes.
The inclination of the orbital planes is 55 degrees.
The orbital period is approximately 85 minutes.
explanation: Each Iridium satellite's three phased-array antenna panels form 48 spot beams that tile its coverage area. The other statements fail: Iridium uses 66 active satellites in six near-polar planes inclined 86.4°, with an orbital period of about 100 minutes.
flag: The pool keys A. Iridium satellites do have 48 spot beams, but each beam is roughly 400 km (about 250 miles) across, not 30 miles. A is still the closest statement; the other three are wrong. Answer A on the exam.

stem: What is the main function of the COSPAS-SARSAT satellite system?
choices: Monitor 121.5 MHz for voice distress calls.
Monitor 406 MHz for distress calls from EPIRBs.
Monitor 1635 MHz for coded distress calls.
Monitor 2197.5 kHz for hexadecimal coded DSC distress messages.
explanation: COSPAS-SARSAT satellites listen for 406 MHz bursts from EPIRBs, ELTs and PLBs and relay them to ground stations (local user terminals) that alert rescue coordination centers. Satellite processing of 121.5 MHz ended in 2009.

stem: How does the COSPAS-SARSAT satellite system determine the position of a ship in distress?
choices: By measuring the Doppler shift of the 406 MHz signal taken at several different points in its orbit.
The EPIRB always transmits its position which is relayed by the satellite to the Local User Terminal.
It takes two different satellites to establish an accurate position.
explanation: As a low-orbiting satellite passes, the received 406 MHz frequency shifts because of Doppler; the timing and amount of that shift during the pass let the ground station compute the beacon's position. Only beacons with built-in GPS also transmit their own coordinates.

stem: What is the orbital altitude of INMARSAT Satellites?
explanation: Inmarsat satellites are geostationary, orbiting about 22,200 miles (35,786 km) above the equator, where one orbit takes a full day and the satellite appears fixed in the sky.

stem: Which of the following describes the INMARSAT Satellite system?
choices: AOR at 35° W, POR-E at 165° W, POR-W at 155° E and IOR at 56.5° E.
AOR-E at 25° W, AOR-W at 85° W, POR at 175° W and IOR at 56.5° E.
AOR-E at 15.5° W, AOR-W at 54° W, POR at 178° E and IOR at 64.5° E.
AOR at 40° W, POR at 178° W, IOR-E at 109° E and IOR-W at 46° E.
explanation: The classic Inmarsat GMDSS layout used four geostationary satellites, one per ocean region: Atlantic Ocean East at 15.5° W, Atlantic Ocean West at 54° W, Pacific Ocean at 178° E and Indian Ocean at 64.5° E.

stem: What are the directional characteristics of the INMARSAT-C SES antenna?
choices: Highly directional parabolic antenna requiring stabilization.
Wide beam width in a cardioid pattern off the front of the antenna.
Very narrow beam width straight-up from the top of the antenna.
explanation: Inmarsat-C's low data rate lets it use a small omnidirectional antenna that needs no aiming or stabilization, so it works on any heading as the vessel rolls and turns.

stem: When engaging in voice communications via an INMARSAT-B terminal, what techniques are used?
choices: CODECs are used to digitize the voice signal.
Noise-blanking must be selected by the operator.
The voice signal must be compressed to fit into the allowed bandwidth.
The voice signal will be expanded at the receiving terminal.
explanation: Inmarsat-B was a digital system, so a codec converted speech into a 16 kbps digital stream for transmission and decoded it back to audio at the far end.

stem: Which of the following statements concerning INMARSAT geostationary satellites is true?
choices: They are in a polar orbit, in order to provide true global coverage.
They are in an equatorial orbit, in order to provide true global coverage.
They provide coverage to vessels in nearly all of the world’s navigable waters.
Vessels sailing in equatorial waters are able to use only one satellite, whereas other vessels are able to choose between at least two satellites.
explanation: Geostationary satellites sit over the equator, and four of them cover the globe except the polar regions above about 70° latitude. That reaches nearly all navigable waters, though not true global coverage, and the satellites are not in polar orbit.

stem: Which of the following conditions can render INMARSAT -B communications impossible?
choices: An obstruction, such as a mast, causing disruption of the signal between the satellite and the SES antenna when the vessel is steering a certain course.
A satellite whose signal is on a low elevation, below the horizon.
Travel beyond the effective radius of the satellite.
explanation: Inmarsat-B's directional dish needs a clear line of sight to the satellite, so a mast blocking it on certain headings, a satellite below the horizon, or sailing beyond the satellite's coverage area will each make communication impossible.

stem: What is the best description for the INMARSAT-C system?
choices: It provides slow speed telex and voice service.
It is a store-and-forward system that provides routine and distress communications.
It is a real-time telex system.
explanation: Inmarsat-C is a store-and-forward data system: messages go in packets to a land earth station, which stores and then delivers them, not in real time. It carries both routine messages and GMDSS distress alerts, and it has no voice.

stem: The INMARSAT mini-M system is a:
choices: Satellite system utilizing spot beams to provide for small craft communications.
explanation: Mini-M was a compact Inmarsat service that used the high-power spot beams of the Inmarsat-3 satellites, which allowed small, light terminals and antennas suitable for yachts and other small craft.
